title: "Residuals"

The Provo regression line assigns each word position a fitted conditional mean. A [**residual**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) is the observed response minus that fitted value.

The [Provo measurements](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data) define that observed response as a mean of log first fixation durations among readers with a retained positive fixation. They also define modeled cloze surprisal as the negative base 2 logarithm of a fitted cloze probability. A residual therefore belongs to the aggregated word position and cannot recover a skipped fixation or a particular reader's discrepancy.

Which Provo patterns remain after the line has been fitted? Residuals for individual positions retain local discrepancies and passage grouping, even though each response was already averaged across readers.

If an observed value $y_i$ exceeds its fitted mean $\widehat y_i$, their difference is positive and the point lies above the line. If it falls below the fitted mean, the difference is negative. Subtracting the fitted mean moves every observation onto a common zero reference while preserving the direction and size of its vertical discrepancy. We perform the subtraction for an observed Provo position below.

$$
e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i.
$$

A positive residual marks a position above the fitted line; a negative residual marks one below it. We can observe this discrepancy after fitting. By contrast, the population error $\varepsilon_i$ remains an unobserved random quantity in the model.

## Computing the Provo regression residuals

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-residuals
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)

provo$fitted_mean_log_ffd <- fitted(fit)
provo$residual <-
  provo$mean_log_ffd - provo$fitted_mean_log_ffd

stopifnot(
  max(abs(provo$residual - residuals(fit))) < 1e-12,
  abs(sum(provo$residual)) < 1e-10
)

summary(provo$residual)
```

The printed summary contains five observed order statistics: the smallest and
largest residuals, the first and third quartiles, and the median. About one
quarter of the residuals fall at or below the first quartile, while the median
is the middle ordered residual. It also prints the arithmetic mean, which is
numerically zero because this fit contains an intercept. These values give a
compact description, though the plot remains necessary because different
distributions can share them.

The first observed subtraction is:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-provo-residual
provo[1L, c(
  "position_id", "mean_log_ffd", "fitted_mean_log_ffd", "residual"
)]
```

Read the output one row at a time. `mean_log_ffd` supplies $y_i$, `fitted_mean_log_ffd` supplies $\widehat y_i$, and `residual` records their difference. Keeping those three columns together is a useful check whenever residuals are computed by hand or transformed in code.

This response remains a mean calculated for each word position over reader log FFDs, as defined for the [Provo response](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data). A residual plot can expose patterns across positions or passages, while reader heterogeneity lies outside a table from which reader identifiers have been removed.

Why do these discrepancies sum to zero? Recall from [least squares](frequentist-linear-regression.qmd#from-discrepancies-to-an-objective) that the fitted coefficients minimize the **error sum of squares (SSE)**, the sum of the squared residuals. With an intercept, moving the entire line slightly upward or downward is one available adjustment. At the minimum, neither movement can reduce squared error. The corresponding intercept equation is

$$
\frac{\partial\operatorname{SSE}}{\partial\beta_0}
=
-2\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)=0.
$$

At the OLS solution, this gives

$$
\sum_i e_i=0.
$$

The Provo regression residuals sum to `r format(sum(provo$residual), scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)`. The zero sum follows from fitting an intercept; it tells us nothing about whether positive and negative discrepancies are equally plausible throughout the predictor range.

## Residual standard error {#residual-standard-error}

The residuals also give us an estimate of the response spread around the fitted
line. Let $p$ be the number of fitted coefficients, including the intercept. In
the current model, $p=2$ because we estimated an intercept and one slope. The
**residual degrees of freedom** are therefore $n-p=n-2$. Recall that [degrees of
freedom](../random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd)
count the independent pieces of information left after accounting for fitted
constraints.

The SSE introduced above is

$$
\operatorname{SSE}=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2.
$$

Dividing by the residual degrees of freedom gives the residual variance
estimate,

$$
s^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p},
$$

and taking the square root gives the **residual standard error (RSE)**,

$$
s
=
\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-p}}.
$$

Why do we subtract two in this regression? The fitted residuals obey two
constraints. The intercept calculation gives $\sum_i e_i=0$, and the slope
calculation gives $\sum_i x_i e_i=0$. Thus the residuals have two fewer ways to
vary freely after we estimate the intercept and slope. In [design matrix
notation](design-matrices.qmd#from-squared-error-to-the-coefficient-estimates),
the same result follows from the rank of the fitted space.

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-residual-standard-error
residual_sse <- sum(provo$residual^2)
number_of_coefficients <- length(coef(fit))
residual_degrees_of_freedom <- nrow(provo) - number_of_coefficients
residual_standard_error <- sqrt(
  residual_sse / residual_degrees_of_freedom
)

stopifnot(
  residual_degrees_of_freedom == df.residual(fit),
  abs(residual_standard_error - summary(fit)$sigma) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(
  error_sum_of_squares = residual_sse,
  observations = nrow(provo),
  fitted_coefficients = number_of_coefficients,
  residual_degrees_of_freedom = residual_degrees_of_freedom,
  residual_standard_error = residual_standard_error
)
```

Substituting the Provo quantities gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
s
&=
\sqrt{
\frac{`r format(residual_sse, digits = 7)`}
{`r residual_degrees_of_freedom`}
} \\
&=
`r format(residual_standard_error, digits = 7)`.
\end{aligned}
$$

Because the response is mean log first fixation duration, the RSE has that same
unit. It estimates the conditional spread of responses around the line under
the common variance model. A coefficient standard error answers another
question: how much an estimated intercept or slope would vary across repeated
samples under the sampling model. We use the RSE to construct those coefficient
standard errors when we turn to [slope uncertainty](linear-regression-uncertainty.qmd).

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-residual-spread
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the Provo residuals. The dashed lines mark one residual standard error below and above zero."
ggplot(provo, aes(residual)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 35L,
    boundary = 0,
    color = "white",
    fill = "grey70"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(-residual_standard_error, residual_standard_error),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linetype = 2,
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(x = "Residual", y = "Number of Provo positions") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The dashed lines merely provide a spread reference. A confidence interval
requires an estimator and sampling distribution, and the RSE formula supplies
no fixed residual coverage probability.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-data-and-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Observed Provo position summaries with the fitted line, followed by the same discrepancies on a residual scale."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
grid$fitted <- predict(fit, newdata = grid)

point_opacity <- 0.2
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Provo regression residuals against fitted values. The blue curve is a descriptive loess smooth."
residual_opacity <- 0.25
ggplot(provo, aes(fitted_mean_log_ffd, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = residual_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(x = "Fitted mean log FFD", y = "Residual") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The smooth bends modestly rather than remaining perfectly horizontal. This
pattern motivates checking the fitted function. Choosing an alternative still
requires a specified comparison.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why does a positive residual place an observation above the line?
2. Why must OLS residuals sum to zero when the model has an intercept?
3. Is a residual the same object as an error term?
4. Why does the RSE use $n-2$ for this fitted line?
5. What model restriction does curvature challenge?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Because $e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i$, a positive value means $y_i>\widehat y_i$ and the point lies above the fitted line. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The intercept normal equation sets the derivative with respect to $\beta_0$ to zero, which requires $\sum_i e_i=0$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. No. A residual is an observed discrepancy after fitting; an error term is an unobserved random quantity in the population model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Estimating the intercept and slope imposes two constraints on the residuals, leaving $n-2$ residual degrees of freedom. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Curvature challenges the restriction that the conditional mean is a straight line in modeled cloze surprisal. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next use the residual spread to derive [slope uncertainty](linear-regression-uncertainty.qmd).
